title: Come, cupbearer
intro: Hafez of Shiraz (about 1315–1390) is the best-loved poet of Iran: his *Divan*, about 500 ghazals gathered after his death, is in almost every Iranian home. The poems are arranged by the last letter of their rhyme, so a ghazal rhyming in *alef* comes first – and this is the one that opens the book. It begins and ends in Arabic. An old story, probably a legend, says the first half-line was borrowed from a verse by the Umayyad caliph Yazid, the most hated man in Shi'i history, and a later poet imagined Hafez answering in a dream that an unbeliever's goods are lawful for a believer to take. In seven couplets the poem moves from the tavern to a dark night at sea, and from a love that 'seemed easy at first' to the poet's advice to himself.

lines.fa: الا یا ایها الساقی ادر کأساً و ناولها / که عشق آسان نمود اول ولی افتاد مشکل‌ها
lines.r: alā yā ayyoh as-sāghi ader ka'san va nāvelhā / ke 'eshgh āsān nemud avval vali oftād moshkel-hā
lines.en: Come, cupbearer, pass the cup round and hand it to me, / for love seemed easy at first, but then came the troubles.
lines.note: The first half-line is Arabic, recited *alā yā ayyohas-sāghi ader ka'san va nāvelhā* – 'Ho, cupbearer! Pass a cup round and hand it over.' In the Persian half, نمود means 'seemed', not 'showed'.
words: to seem easy (نمودن 'to seem, to appear')

lines.fa: به بوی نافه‌ای کاخر صبا زان طره بگشاید / ز تاب جعد مشکینش چه خون افتاد در دل‌ها
lines.r: be bu-ye nāfe-i kākhar sabā zān torre begshāyad / ze tāb-e ja'd-e moshkin-ash che khun oftād dar del-hā
lines.en: Waiting for the musk the east wind will at last shake loose from that lock of hair, / how many hearts have bled at the twist of those musky curls!
lines.note: نافه is the musk pod of the musk deer; the beloved's dark, scented hair is compared to it. صبا *sabā*, the morning breeze from the east, carries scents and messages between lovers all through Hafez.
words: in hope of (lit. 'for the scent of')
that in the end – که + آخر
the east wind, the morning breeze

lines.fa: مرا در منزل جانان چه امن عیش چون هر دم / جرس فریاد می‌دارد که بربندید محمل‌ها
lines.r: marā dar manzel-e jānān che amn-e 'eysh chon har dam / jaras faryād mi-dārad ke barbandid mahmel-hā
lines.en: What peace can I enjoy at my beloved's house, when every moment / the caravan bell cries out: 'Tie on the litters, we are moving on!'
words: stopping place on a journey; house
a litter carried by a camel

lines.fa: به می سجاده رنگین کن گرت پیر مغان گوید / که سالک بی‌خبر نبود ز راه و رسم منزل‌ها
lines.r: be mey sajjāde rangin kon gar-at pir-e moghān guyad / ke sālek bi-khabar nabvad ze rāh o rasm-e manzel-hā
lines.en: Stain your prayer rug with wine if the old Magian master tells you to, / for one who travels the path knows its ways and its stations.
lines.note: In Hafez the *pir-e moghān*, the old Zoroastrian who keeps the tavern, stands for a spiritual guide who knows more than the official preachers. The couplet is a famous provocation: obey the true master, even if he tells you to stain the prayer rug.
words: if … you – گر + ـت; the ـت belongs to the verb: 'if he tells you'
the old master of the Magians, the tavern keeper
is not – the old present of بودن (today نیست)

lines.fa: شب تاریک و بیم موج و گردابی چنین هایل / کجا دانند حال ما سبکباران ساحل‌ها
lines.r: shab-e tārik o bim-e mowj o gerdābi chonin hāyel / kojā dānand hāl-e mā sabokbārān-e sāhel-hā
lines.en: A dark night, the fear of the waves and a whirlpool so terrible – / how could those who stroll lightly on the shore know how we fare?

lines.fa: همه کارم ز خودکامی به بدنامی کشید آخر / نهان کی ماند آن رازی کز او سازند محفل‌ها
lines.r: hame kār-am ze khodkāmi be badnāmi keshid ākhar / nahān key mānad ān rāzi kaz u sāzand mahfel-hā
lines.en: Doing as I pleased, I ended up with a bad name; / how can a secret stay hidden when people gather to talk about it?
words: all my affairs, everything I did
to lead to, to end in
that from it – که + از او

lines.fa: حضوری گر همی‌خواهی از او غایب مشو حافظ / متی ما تلق من تهوی دع الدنیا و اهملها
lines.r: hozuri gar hami-khāhi az u ghāyeb masho hāfez / matā mā talgha man tahvā da' ed-donyā va ahmelhā
lines.en: If you want to be in his presence, Hafez, do not be absent from him: / when you meet the one you love, leave the world and let it go.
lines.note: The last half-line is Arabic again, recited *matā mā talgha man tahvā da'ed-donyā va ahmelhā* – 'whenever you meet the one you desire, leave the world and neglect it'. Hafez names himself in the last couplet of nearly every ghazal; this signature is called the تخلص *takhallos*.
words: you want – همی is the old form of می‌
do not become – the old negative imperative (today نشو)
whenever you meet the one you love (Arabic)
leave the world and neglect it (Arabic)

commentary:
**The images.** Hafez braids three worlds together. There is the tavern: the cupbearer, the wine, the old Magian master, a prayer rug stained red. There is the beloved, whose musky curls make lovers' hearts bleed. And there is the journey: the caravan bell that will not let anyone rest, the night sea with its whirlpool. All three say the same thing – love looked easy at the start, and it is not. Read one way, the beloved is God and the wine is the joy of being near him; read another, this is simply a lover's poem. Hafez never lets you settle on one reading for good, and that is half of his charm.

**The rhythm.** The ghazal is in *hazaj*, the commonest metre of Persian: four even steps to the half-line, *da-DUM-DUM-DUM* four times over. You can hear it in the first Persian words of the poem: *ke 'esh-ghā-sān ne-mud av-val*. Every couplet ends in the same rhyme – [[ناولها|nāvelhā]], [[مشکل‌ها|moshkel-hā]], [[دل‌ها|del-hā]], [[محمل‌ها|mahmel-hā]] – so that the Persian plural [[ها|-hā]] rhymes with the Arabic [[ها|-hā]] 'it'.

**The grammar.** Two Arabic half-lines frame the poem, but the Persian between them is close to today's. Look for [[ز|ze]] for [[از|az]], [[گر|gar]] for [[اگر|agar]], [[کز|kaz]] for [[که از|ke az]], [[همی‌خواهی|hami-khāhi]] for [[می‌خواهی|mi-khāhi]], [[مشو|masho]] for [[نشو|nasho]] and [[نبود|nabvad]] for [[نیست|nist]]. In [[گرت پیر مغان گوید|gar-at pir-e moghān guyad]] the little [[ـت|-at]] 'you' hangs on the first word of the clause but belongs to the verb: 'if the old master tells you'. Couplet 6 in modern prose: [[سرانجام همه‌ی کارهایم از خودکامی به بدنامی کشید؛ رازی که درباره‌اش محفل‌ها می‌سازند چطور پنهان می‌ماند؟|saranjām hame-ye kār-hā-yam az khodkāmi be badnāmi keshid; rāzi ke darbāre-ash mahfel-hā mi-sāzand chetowr penhān mi-mānad?]]

**Using it.** Iranians open the *Divan* at random to take a *fāl*, an omen, especially on Yalda, the longest night of the year – and whoever opens it at the first page meets this ghazal. [[عشق آسان نمود اول ولی افتاد مشکل‌ها|'eshgh āsān nemud avval vali oftād moshkel-hā]] is said of any plan that turned out harder than it looked, and [[سبکباران ساحل‌ها|sabokbārān-e sāhel-hā]] of people who judge a struggle from a safe distance.
